tells: Photoreal, physically lit macro worlds: a crater pooling a nebula, a nautilus shell lit from inside on sand. Each has real material, depth of field and atmospheric light.

A clear thread of scale-matching runs through it. Crater becomes nebula, the shell's spiral becomes an accretion disc, and the sequence ends on an eye-nebula. That is choreographed visual rhyming from frame to frame, not a set of separate shots.
The credits are small, tracked caps tucked into negative space so they don't fight the image. That is standard broadcast title craft.
The ending lockup is built around the image. Widely spaced COSMOS letters flank the pupil, so the O sits on the iris. The type and the picture work as one idea.
Weaknesses: the eye-nebula is a well-worn space-documentary trope, and the typeface is a fairly generic geometric sans.
gaps: The closing eye/nebula metaphor is the most predictable image in the piece. A stranger final reveal would lift originality.
The type is functional rather than authored. A custom or more characterful title face would give the lockup a point of view.
The palette leans on stock 'cosmic orange/teal'. A more deliberate, restricted grade would make it more distinctive.

defects: The year numerals (1990, 2011) are mostly covered by ice and ocean, so they are hard to read. The 2011 frame barely reads as a year at all.
The top-left captions sit straight on the cracked ice with no backing plate or shadow. Crack lines run through the letters ('September 2011: 4.56 million km²').
The 3.57 numeral is cut off by the floe edges. Its caption ('million km² in September 2012…') begins mid-sentence, so the number and the unit are visually disconnected.
In the pairs, the floes and the chart barely change between frames 1/6 s apart. Long stretches look nearly static, including the 12.5 s shot, where the change per second falls to about 8 at the end.
The bar chart frame is static apart from bars filling in. The bars have no stagger easing or settle, and nothing in the frame moves once it is built.
The closing Greenland frame has tiny footer source text and a thin orange outline that will alias or shimmer at delivery size.
The opening frame carries two lines of explanatory caption, so it reads as an infographic rather than a title moment.
gaps: Motion: the ice should behave like a physical material. Floes should crack, drift, rotate, and break apart with inertia and secondary motion, instead of slow dissolves between static states. The chart and the Greenland reveal need choreographed builds with overshoot and settle, and the 12.5 s held shot needs internal camera or material movement.

Arc and pace: the emotional peak (2012 at 3.57) lands at about 43% of the running time. The film then flattens into a slow chart and a quiet map. To build toward a 60-80% climax, the edit should compress the year sequence into faster, accelerating cuts and make the Greenland comparison the hit.

Sound: the score is a mostly static drone of stacked harmonics with only three transient hits (about 4.3 s, 13.2 s and 18.2 s) and one broadband swell (about 24-26.5 s). There is no foley-level ice sound design (cracks, groans, water) and little dynamic shaping. Picture changes that do not land on a hit go without any audio accent.
